{{Short description|Description in spectral theory}}
In [[mathematics]], especially [[spectral theory]], '''Weyl's law''' describes the asymptotic behavior of eigenvalues of the [[Laplace–Beltrami operator]]. This description was discovered in 1911 (in the <math>d=2,3</math> case) by [[Hermann Weyl]] for eigenvalues for the Laplace–Beltrami operator acting on functions that vanish at the boundary of a bounded domain <math> \Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d</math>. In particular, he proved that the number, <math> N(\lambda)</math>, of [[Dirichlet eigenvalue]]s (counting their multiplicities) less than or equal to <math>\lambda</math> satisfies
:<math>
\lim_{\lambda \rightarrow \infty} \frac{N(\lambda)}{\lambda^{d/2}} = (2\pi)^{-d} \omega_d \mathrm{vol}(\Omega)
</math>
where  <math>\omega_d</math> is a [[Volume of an n-ball|volume of the unit ball]] in <math>\mathbb{R}^d</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Weyl |first=Hermann |url=https://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/id/PPN252457811_1911?tify={%22pages%22:[122,123],%22panX%22:0.912,%22panY%22:0.705,%22view%22:%22fulltext%22,%22zoom%22:0.363} |title=Über die asymptotische Verteilung der Eigenwerte |journal=Nachrichten der Königlichen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen |pages=110–117 |year=1911 }}</ref> In 1912 he provided a new proof based on [[variational methods]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=Das asymptotische Verteilungsgesetz linearen partiellen Differentialgleichungen |journal=[[Mathematische Annalen]] |volume=71 |pages=441–479 |year=1912 |doi=10.1007/BF01456804 |s2cid=120278241 |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1526112 }}</ref><ref>For a proof in English, see {{cite book |title=Partial Differential Equations |first=Walter A. |last=Strauss |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |year=2008 }} See chapter 11.</ref> Weyl's law can be extended to closed [[Riemannian manifold]]s, where another proof can be given using the [[Minakshisundaram–Pleijel zeta function#Applications|Minakshisundaram–Pleijel zeta function]]. 

==Generalizations==
The Weyl law has been extended to more general domains and operators.  For the Schrödinger operator
:<math>
H=-h^2 \Delta + V(x)
</math>
it was extended to
:<math>
N(E,h)\sim (2\pi h)^{-d}  \int _{\{ |\xi|^2 + V(x)<E \}} dx\, d\xi
</math>
as <math>E </math> tending to <math>+\infty</math> or to a bottom of essential spectrum and/or <math>h\to +0</math>.
<ref>See Theorem A.2.1 in {{cite book |title=Pseudodifferential Operators and Spectral Theory |first=Mikhail |last=Shubin |publisher=Springer-Verlag |year=2001 |ISBN=978-3-540-41195-6 }}</ref>
Here <math>N(E,h)</math> is the number of eigenvalues of <math>H</math> below <math>E</math> unless there is essential spectrum below <math>E</math> in which case <math>N(E,h)=+\infty</math>.

In the development of [[spectral asymptotics]], the crucial role was played by [[variational methods]] and [[microlocal analysis]].

==Counter-examples==
The extended Weyl law fails in certain situations. In particular, the extended Weyl law "claims" that there is no [[essential spectrum]]  if and only if  the right-hand expression is finite for all <math>E</math>.

If one considers domains with cusps (i.e. "shrinking exits to infinity") then the (extended) Weyl law claims that there is no essential spectrum if and only if the volume is finite. However for the Dirichlet Laplacian there is no essential spectrum even if the volume is infinite as long as cusps shrinks at infinity (so the finiteness of the volume is not necessary).

On the other hand, for the Neumann Laplacian there is an essential spectrum unless cusps shrinks at infinity faster than the negative exponent (so the finiteness of the volume is not sufficient).

==Weyl conjecture==
Weyl conjectured that
:<math>
N(\lambda)= (2\pi)^{-d}\lambda ^{d/2} \omega_d \mathrm{vol} (\Omega)\mp \frac{1}{4} (2\pi)^{1-d}\omega_{d - 1}\lambda ^{(d-1)/2}\mathrm{area} (\partial \Omega) +o (\lambda ^{(d-1)/2})
</math>

where the remainder term is negative for Dirichlet boundary conditions and positive for Neumann.
The remainder estimate was improved upon by many mathematicians.

In 1922, [[Richard Courant]] proved a bound of <math>O(\lambda^{(d-1)/2}\log \lambda)</math>.
In 1952, [[Boris Levitan]] proved the tighter bound of <math>O(\lambda^{(d-1)/2})</math> for compact closed manifolds. [[Robert Thomas Seeley|Robert Seeley]] extended this to include certain Euclidean domains in 1978.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Seeley | first1=Robert | authorlink1=Robert Thomas Seeley
| title=A sharp asymptotic estimate for the eigenvalues of the Laplacian in a domain of <math>\mathbf{R}^3</math>
| journal=[[Advances in Mathematics]]
| volume=102
| issue=3
| pages=244–264
| date=1978
| doi=10.1016/0001-8708(78)90013-0 | doi-access=free}}</ref>
In 1975, [[Hans Duistermaat]] and [[Victor Guillemin]] proved the bound of
<math>o(\lambda ^{(d-1)/2})</math> when the set of periodic bicharacteristics has measure 0.<ref>The spectrum of positive elliptic operators and periodic bicharacteristics. [[Inventiones Mathematicae]], 29(1):37–79 (1975).</ref>  This was finally generalized by [[Victor Ivrii]] in 1980.<ref>Second term of the spectral asymptotic expansion for the Laplace–Beltrami operator on manifold with boundary. Functional Analysis and Its Applications 14(2):98–106 (1980).</ref>  This generalization assumes that the set of periodic trajectories of a billiard in <math>\Omega</math> has measure 0, which Ivrii conjectured is fulfilled for all bounded Euclidean domains with smooth boundaries.  Since then, similar results have been obtained for wider classes of operators.

==Uses in black body radiation==
In a cubed hollow cavity with length size <math>L</math> and volume <math>V=L^3</math> the [[density of states]] of the electromagnetic radiation with angular frequency <math>\omega</math> is given by
:<math>
g(\omega)=\frac{V\omega^2}{\pi^2c^3}
</math>
where <math>c</math> is the speed of light. Weyl's law can be used to show that this density of states applies to cavities of any shape if they are ''sufficiently large''.<ref>{{cite |title=Plankc's Radiation Law for Finite Cavities and Related Problems |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/chapter/edited-volume/abs/pii/B9780080208800500039 }}</ref>
